stem: After independence, India adopted the approach of __________ to guide its economic development.
solution: After independence, India adopted the approach of economic planning — through a series of Five Year Plans — to guide and direct its economic development. Under this approach, the government drew up plans setting out the goals and the allocation of resources for the economy over five-year periods, with the aim of developing the country in a planned, coordinated way. India chose a 'mixed economy' (combining planning and a public sector with a private sector), following a middle path between pure capitalism and pure socialism. Understanding that India adopted economic planning (Five Year Plans) is a key prelims point. After independence, India adopted economic planning through Five Year Plans to guide its development.

stem: The body set up in 1950 to formulate India's Five Year Plans was the:
solution: The Planning Commission was the body set up in 1950 (with the Prime Minister as its chairman) to formulate and oversee India's Five Year Plans and to guide the country's economic planning and development. It assessed the country's resources and prepared the plans, setting the goals and allocating resources. (The Planning Commission functioned until 2014, when it was replaced by the NITI Aayog.) Understanding that the Planning Commission (set up 1950) made the Five Year Plans is a prelims point. The Planning Commission, set up in 1950, was the body that formulated India's Five Year Plans.

stem: India's First Five Year Plan (1951–56) gave the highest priority to the development of:
solution: India's First Five Year Plan (1951–56) gave the highest priority to the development of agriculture, including irrigation and power. This was because agriculture was in a poor, stagnant state (and India faced food shortages), so raising agricultural production (to feed the people and provide raw materials) was the most urgent need. The First Plan (based on the Harrod-Domar model) focused on rebuilding agriculture, irrigation projects (like large dams), and refugee rehabilitation, and it was largely successful in raising farm output. Understanding that the First Plan prioritised agriculture is a prelims point. The First Five Year Plan (1951–56) gave the highest priority to agriculture (and irrigation).

stem: India's Second Five Year Plan (1956–61), based on the Mahalanobis model, emphasised the rapid development of:
solution: India's Second Five Year Plan (1956–61) emphasised the rapid development of heavy (basic) industries — the industries that produce machines, steel, and other capital goods needed to build up the rest of the economy. It was based on the model devised by the statistician P.C. Mahalanobis (so it is called the Mahalanobis Plan/model), which argued that rapid industrialisation, led by heavy industry in the public sector, was the key to long-term growth and self-reliance. Under this plan, major public-sector heavy industries (like steel plants) were set up. This laid the foundation of India's industrial base. Understanding that the Second Plan (Mahalanobis) emphasised heavy industry is a key prelims point. The Second Five Year Plan (1956–61), based on the Mahalanobis model, emphasised the rapid development of heavy (basic) industries.

stem: The statistician who designed the strategy of the Second Five Year Plan (emphasising heavy industry) was:
solution: P.C. Mahalanobis — the eminent statistician (founder of the Indian Statistical Institute) — designed the strategy (model) of the Second Five Year Plan, which emphasised the rapid development of heavy and basic industries in the public sector as the path to industrialisation and self-reliance. He is often called the 'architect of Indian planning' (for the second plan onward). His model shaped India's industrialisation strategy for decades. Understanding that P.C. Mahalanobis designed the Second Plan strategy is a prelims point. P.C. Mahalanobis, the statistician, designed the heavy-industry strategy of the Second Five Year Plan.

stem: The type of economy that India adopted (with both a public sector and a private sector coexisting) is called a:
solution: India adopted a mixed economy — an economic system in which both the public sector (government-owned enterprises) and the private sector (privately-owned businesses) coexist and operate together. India chose this middle path between pure capitalism (a purely private, free-market economy) and pure socialism (a fully state-controlled/command economy): the state took the leading role in key/basic industries and planning (the public sector), while private enterprise was allowed (but regulated) in many areas. This reflected India's goals of growth with social justice and self-reliance. Understanding that India adopted a mixed economy is a key prelims point. India adopted a mixed economy, with both the public and private sectors coexisting.

stem: The main goals (objectives) of India's Five Year Plans included growth, modernisation, self-reliance, and:
solution: The four main goals (objectives) of India's Five Year Plans were: (1) growth — increasing the country's output (Gross Domestic Product) and the availability of goods and services; (2) modernisation — adopting new technology and changing social outlook (e.g., empowering women); (3) self-reliance — being able to stand on one's own (avoiding dependence on imports and foreign aid, especially for essentials); and (4) equity — ensuring that the benefits of growth reached all sections of society and reducing inequality and poverty (social justice). So growth, modernisation, self-reliance, and equity together were the goals — reflecting the aim of 'growth with social justice'. Understanding these four plan goals is a key prelims point. The goals of the Five Year Plans were growth, modernisation, self-reliance, and equity (social justice).

stem: The goal of 'self-reliance' in India's planning meant:
options: Depending heavily on imports and foreign aid
Reducing dependence on foreign countries/imports (especially for food and key goods) by producing them within India
solution: The goal of 'self-reliance' (self-sufficiency) in India's planning meant reducing India's dependence on foreign countries — particularly on imports of food and other essential goods, and on foreign aid — by producing these things within the country itself. This was considered important both economically (to avoid the costs and instability of imports) and politically (a newly independent nation did not want to be dependent on, or vulnerable to, foreign powers). So India aimed to become self-reliant — for example, achieving self-sufficiency in food grains (via the Green Revolution) and building up its own industries (via import substitution). Understanding the meaning of self-reliance is a prelims point. Self-reliance meant reducing India's dependence on foreign imports/aid by producing goods (especially food and essentials) within the country.

stem: To achieve self-reliance in industry, India followed a policy of __________ — replacing imports with goods produced domestically (behind high tariffs and protection).
solution: To achieve self-reliance in industry, India followed the policy of import substitution — the strategy of replacing (substituting) imported goods with goods produced within the country (domestically), so as to reduce dependence on imports and to develop domestic industries. To make this work, the government protected the domestic industries from foreign competition through high tariffs (duties) on imports and quotas/restrictions on imports (an 'inward-looking' trade strategy). The idea was that, sheltered from foreign competition, Indian industries would grow and the country would become self-reliant. (This is contrasted with 'export promotion', an outward-looking strategy.) Understanding import substitution (protectionist self-reliance strategy) is a key prelims point. India followed import substitution — replacing imports with domestically-produced goods, behind high tariffs — to achieve self-reliance.

stem: The revolution that made India self-sufficient in food grains (through the use of high-yielding variety seeds, fertilisers, and irrigation) was the:
solution: The Green Revolution was the great increase in food-grain production in India (from the mid-1960s onward) that made the country self-sufficient in food grains, ending its dependence on food imports and food shortages. It was achieved through the use of high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds (especially of wheat and rice), along with chemical fertilisers, pesticides, assured irrigation, and modern farming methods. The Green Revolution dramatically raised yields (especially of wheat, and especially in states like Punjab, Haryana, and western Uttar Pradesh) and transformed Indian agriculture. Understanding that the Green Revolution made India self-sufficient in food grains is a key prelims point. The Green Revolution, using HYV seeds, fertilisers, and irrigation, made India self-sufficient in food grains.

stem: A key input responsible for the Green Revolution was the introduction of __________ seeds.
solution: A key input responsible for the Green Revolution was the introduction of high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds — specially bred seeds (of wheat and rice) that give much higher yields (more output per hectare) than the traditional seeds. These HYV seeds, however, needed the right conditions to give their high yields: plenty of water (assured irrigation), chemical fertilisers, and pesticides. When these inputs were provided together, food-grain production rose dramatically. So the HYV seeds (with fertilisers and irrigation) were at the heart of the Green Revolution. Understanding the role of HYV seeds is a prelims point. The Green Revolution was driven by high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds (used with fertilisers and irrigation).

stem: In the FIRST phase of the Green Revolution, the increase in production was mainly confined to:
options: all crops equally, all over India
wheat (and a few states like Punjab, Haryana, and western UP)
solution: In the first phase of the Green Revolution (the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s), the increase in production was mainly confined to wheat, and it was largely confined to a few, more prosperous and well-irrigated states — Punjab, Haryana, and western Uttar Pradesh. This was because these regions had the assured irrigation and resources needed for the HYV technology. In the later (second) phase, the Green Revolution spread to more crops (including rice) and more states. Understanding that the first phase was confined mainly to wheat and a few states is a prelims point. In the first phase, the Green Revolution's gains were mainly in wheat and in a few states (Punjab, Haryana, western UP).

stem: The system by which the government purchases food grains from farmers at a guaranteed 'minimum support price' (MSP) and maintains a buffer stock is important for:
options: ensuring a fair price to farmers and food security (distributing food through the public distribution system)
solution: The system by which the government purchases (procures) food grains from farmers at a guaranteed 'Minimum Support Price' (MSP), and stores them as a 'buffer stock', is important for two main reasons: (1) it ensures a fair, remunerative price to the farmers (protecting them from a fall in prices, and giving them an incentive to produce more); and (2) it helps ensure food security — the buffer stock of grain is used to supply food at affordable prices to the poor (through the Public Distribution System — the ration shops) and to meet shortages or emergencies (like droughts). So the MSP and buffer-stock system supports both the farmers and the food security of the country. Understanding the MSP/buffer-stock system is a prelims point. The MSP and buffer-stock system ensures fair prices to farmers and food security (through the public distribution system).

stem: The removal of intermediaries (like zamindars) between the state and the cultivators, so that the actual tillers became the owners of the land, was a key __________ reform after independence.
solution: The abolition of intermediaries (like the zamindars) — removing the middlemen between the state and the actual cultivators, so that the tillers of the soil became the owners of the land they cultivated — was a key part of the land reforms (agrarian reforms) undertaken after independence. Land reforms aimed to change the exploitative agrarian structure inherited from colonial rule and to promote equity and productivity in agriculture. The abolition of intermediaries was the most successful of these reforms (it did remove the zamindars in most areas), though other land reforms (like land-ceiling laws to redistribute land to the landless) were only partly successful. Understanding the abolition of intermediaries (a land reform) is a prelims point. The abolition of intermediaries (like zamindars), making the tillers the owners, was a key land (agrarian) reform after independence.

stem: The 'land ceiling' reform aimed to:
options: increase the land held by big landlords
fix a maximum limit on the land a person/family could own, and redistribute the surplus land to the landless
give all land to the government
solution: The 'land ceiling' reform aimed to fix a maximum limit (a ceiling) on the amount of land that a single person or family could own, so that the surplus land (above this ceiling) could be taken over and redistributed to the landless and poor farmers. The goal was to reduce the concentration of land ownership (the inequality of landholdings) and to give land to the landless (promoting equity). However, this reform was only partly successful — it was poorly implemented in many states, and big landowners often evaded the ceiling (e.g., by transferring land to relatives or through legal loopholes). Understanding the land-ceiling reform (its aim and limited success) is a prelims point. The land-ceiling reform aimed to fix a maximum limit on landholding and redistribute the surplus land to the landless.

stem: During 1950–1990, the Indian economy was heavily REGULATED by the government through a system of licences and permits, popularly called the:
solution: During 1950–1990, the Indian economy was heavily regulated (controlled) by the government through an elaborate system of industrial licences, permits, and quotas — a business needed government licences/permits to start or expand an industry, to produce, to import, etc. This regime of pervasive controls was popularly and critically called the 'License-Permit-Quota Raj' (the 'License Raj'). It was intended to direct and control the economy in line with the plans, but it led to red tape, delays, corruption, inefficiency, and a lack of competition — which is why it was later criticised and dismantled (in the 1991 reforms). Understanding the License-Permit-Quota Raj is a key prelims point. The heavily-regulated economy of 1950–1990, controlled through licences and permits, was called the 'License-Permit-Quota Raj'.

stem: The government reserved the production of many goods for the __________ sector, to protect small producers and generate employment.
solution: The government reserved the production of many goods exclusively for the small-scale industries (SSI) sector — meaning that certain items could be produced only by small-scale units (and not by large industries). This policy of reservation was intended to protect and promote small producers (small-scale and cottage industries), because they generate a lot of employment (being labour-intensive) and help spread industry and incomes more widely (promoting equity). So small-scale industries were given protection and encouragement. Understanding the reservation of goods for small-scale industries is a prelims point. Many goods were reserved for production by the small-scale industries sector, to protect small producers and generate employment.

stem: The Green Revolution, while making India self-sufficient in food, also had some NEGATIVE effects, such as:
options: increasing regional and income inequalities (benefiting mainly the richer farmers/states), and causing environmental problems (from overuse of chemicals and water)
making India dependent on food imports
solution: The Green Revolution, while a great success in making India self-sufficient in food grains, also had some negative effects/criticisms: (1) it increased inequalities — it benefited mainly the richer, larger farmers (who could afford the costly inputs — HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation) and the more prosperous, well-irrigated regions (like Punjab, Haryana), widening the gap between rich and poor farmers and between regions; and (2) it caused environmental problems — the overuse of chemical fertilisers and pesticides degraded and polluted the soil and water, and the heavy use of water (for the water-intensive HYV crops) depleted groundwater. So the Green Revolution had costs alongside its benefits. Understanding the negative effects of the Green Revolution (inequality, environmental harm) is a prelims point. The Green Revolution increased regional and income inequalities and caused environmental problems (from overuse of chemicals and water).

stem: By 1990, a major criticism of the public sector (government-owned enterprises) in India was that many of them were:
options: inefficient and loss-making (a drain on the government), due to over-manning, poor management, and lack of competition
solution: By 1990, a major criticism of the public sector (the government-owned enterprises, which had been greatly expanded under planning) was that many of them had become inefficient and loss-making — a drain on the government's resources — rather than generating the surplus/profits needed to finance further development. The reasons included: over-manning (employing more people than needed); poor management and lack of accountability; the lack of competition (as they were protected monopolies with no incentive to be efficient); political interference; and continuing to run even chronically loss-making units. This poor performance of the public sector was one of the factors that led to the economic reforms of 1991. Understanding the criticism of the inefficient, loss-making public sector is a prelims point. By 1990, many public-sector enterprises were criticised as inefficient and loss-making, due to over-manning, poor management, and lack of competition.

stem: Assertion (A): The heavy protection of Indian industries (import substitution, licensing) had drawbacks. Reason (R): Protected from competition, many industries had little incentive to improve their efficiency or the quality of their products. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the heavy protection of Indian industries (through import substitution, high tariffs, and industrial licensing) had significant drawbacks. And the reason is (R) that, being protected from both foreign competition (by the import barriers) and, often, domestic competition (by the licensing system, which limited who could produce), many Indian industries had little incentive or pressure to improve their efficiency, reduce their costs, or improve the quality of their products (they had a captive, sheltered market regardless). This led to inefficient, high-cost, poor-quality production. So the lack of competitive pressure (R) is exactly why the protection had these drawbacks (A). Understanding this criticism of protectionism is a prelims point. Protection had drawbacks because, sheltered from competition, industries had little incentive to improve efficiency or product quality.

stem: The type of society that India's planners (especially Nehru) aimed to build — combining growth with social justice and a large role for the state — was described as a 'socialist pattern of society'. This reflected the influence of:
options: socialist ideas (a large role for the state and concern for equity), within a democratic framework
solution: India's planners (especially Jawaharlal Nehru, and following the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956) aimed to build a 'socialist pattern of society' — a society combining economic growth with social justice/equity, in which the state (public sector) would play a large, leading role in the economy (owning and controlling key industries and directing development), so as to reduce inequalities and ensure that development benefited all. This reflected the influence of socialist ideas (a big role for the state, concern for the poor and for equity, control over the 'commanding heights' of the economy) — but pursued within a democratic framework (not the authoritarian, fully state-controlled model of the communist countries). This is why India chose a mixed economy leaning toward socialism. Understanding the 'socialist pattern of society' goal is a prelims point. India aimed to build a 'socialist pattern of society' — growth with social justice and a large state role — reflecting socialist ideas within a democratic framework.

stem: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 (IPR 1956) classified industries into three categories. The FIRST category (Schedule A) was reserved exclusively for the:
solution: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 (IPR 1956), a landmark document of India's industrial policy, classified industries into three categories (schedules): Schedule A — industries reserved exclusively for the state (public sector), i.e., to be developed only by the government (this included the most important, basic, and strategic industries — like arms, atomic energy, railways, heavy industries); Schedule B — industries in which the state would increasingly own and set up new units, but the private sector could also operate (a mixed category); and Schedule C — all the remaining industries, left to the private sector (but still subject to government regulation/licensing). So IPR 1956 gave the public sector a dominant, expanding role (the 'commanding heights'), reflecting the socialist pattern. Understanding IPR 1956's three schedules (Schedule A reserved for the state) is a prelims point. Under IPR 1956, Schedule A industries were reserved exclusively for the state (public sector).

stem: The public sector was to control the 'commanding heights' of the economy, meaning it would dominate the:
options: key/strategic and basic industries and infrastructure (steel, power, heavy industry, railways, etc.)
solution: The idea that the public sector should control the 'commanding heights' of the economy meant that the government (public sector) would own and dominate the key, strategic, and basic industries and infrastructure — such as steel, heavy engineering, power (electricity), coal, oil, railways, defence, banking, and other crucial/basic sectors — which are vital to the whole economy. By controlling these 'commanding heights', the state could guide and direct the overall course of the economy (in line with the plans and the socialist pattern), build the essential foundation for industrialisation, and prevent the concentration of economic power in private hands. This was a central feature of India's development strategy from 1950 to 1990. Understanding the 'commanding heights' role of the public sector is a prelims point. Controlling the 'commanding heights' meant the public sector would dominate the key, strategic, and basic industries and infrastructure.

stem: The very low, slow rate of economic growth (around 3.5% a year) that India experienced during much of the planning period (1950s–1980s) was disparagingly called the:
solution: The low, slow rate of economic growth — about 3.5% a year for the aggregate economy (and only about 1–1.5% in per-capita terms) — that India experienced during much of the planning period (from the 1950s to about 1980) was disparagingly nicknamed the 'Hindu rate of growth' (a term coined by the economist Raj Krishna). The name (which has nothing to do with the Hindu religion) was used to express frustration at the persistently sluggish, mediocre growth of the Indian economy — much slower than the fast-growing East Asian economies — despite the planning effort. This slow growth (and the failure to make a big dent in poverty) was a key criticism of the planning era. Understanding the 'Hindu rate of growth' is a prelims point. The slow ~3.5% growth of India's economy during the planning era was called the 'Hindu rate of growth'.

stem: The First Five Year Plan was based on the growth model of:
solution: The First Five Year Plan (1951–56) was based on the Harrod-Domar growth model. This model emphasises that the rate of economic growth depends on the level of saving and investment (higher saving and investment → higher growth) — it stresses capital accumulation as the key to growth. So the First Plan focused on raising investment (in agriculture, irrigation, and infrastructure). (The Second Plan, by contrast, was based on the Mahalanobis model, which emphasised heavy industry.) Understanding that the First Plan used the Harrod-Domar model is a prelims point. The First Five Year Plan was based on the Harrod-Domar growth model (emphasising saving and investment).

stem: The amount of farm produce that a farmer sells in the market (over and above what the family keeps for its own consumption) is called the:
solution: The marketable surplus is the portion of the farm produce (like food grains) that the farmer sells in the market — that is, the amount left over and sold after keeping aside what the farm family needs for its own consumption (and for seed, etc.). The marketable surplus is important because it is what feeds the non-farming population (in the cities and towns) and supplies raw materials to industry. The Green Revolution increased the marketable surplus (as production rose, farmers had more to sell), which helped feed the growing urban population and supported the country's food security. Understanding the marketable surplus is a prelims point. The marketable surplus is the part of the farm produce that the farmer sells in the market, after keeping what the family consumes.

stem: The government agency that procures, stores, and distributes food grains (maintaining the buffer stock) in India is the:
solution: The Food Corporation of India (FCI) is the government agency responsible for procuring (buying) food grains from farmers (at the Minimum Support Price), storing them (maintaining the buffer stock of grain), and distributing them — supplying grain to the Public Distribution System (the ration/fair-price shops) and for other needs. The FCI (set up in 1965) thus plays a central role in India's food-security system, in supporting farmers' prices, and in managing the buffer stock. Understanding the FCI's role (procurement, storage, distribution of food grains) is a prelims point. The Food Corporation of India (FCI) procures, stores, and distributes food grains and maintains the buffer stock.

stem: The system of distributing essential goods (like food grains, sugar, kerosene) to the people at subsidised prices through 'ration shops' (fair-price shops) is called the:
solution: The Public Distribution System (PDS) is the government system of distributing essential commodities — such as food grains (wheat and rice), sugar, and kerosene — to the people (especially the poor) at subsidised (low, affordable) prices, through a network of 'ration shops' or 'fair-price shops'. The PDS (supplied from the government's buffer stock, via the FCI) is a key instrument of India's food-security policy, aimed at ensuring that even the poor can obtain essential food and goods at affordable prices. Understanding the PDS (subsidised distribution through ration shops) is a prelims point. The Public Distribution System (PDS) distributes essential goods at subsidised prices through fair-price (ration) shops.

stem: The abolition of intermediaries (zamindars) was the MOST successful land reform, but the land-ceiling reform was largely a failure because:
options: of poor implementation, legal loopholes, and delays that allowed big landowners to evade the ceiling
the ceiling was set too low
solution: Among the land reforms, the abolition of intermediaries (zamindars) was the most successful (it did largely remove the zamindars in most regions). But the land-ceiling reform (fixing a maximum limit on landholding and redistributing the surplus to the landless) was largely a failure — for reasons such as: poor and half-hearted implementation by the states; legal loopholes and long delays in the laws (which the big landowners exploited); the practice of 'benami' transfers (big landowners transferring land, on paper, to relatives and others to stay under the ceiling); and litigation. As a result, little surplus land was actually redistributed, and land ownership remained unequal in many areas. Understanding why the land-ceiling reform failed is a prelims point. The land-ceiling reform largely failed due to poor implementation, legal loopholes, and delays that let big landowners evade it.

stem: The 'White Revolution' (Operation Flood), which made India a leading producer of milk, was led by:
solution: The 'White Revolution' (also called Operation Flood) — the programme that dramatically increased India's milk production and made India the world's largest producer of milk, through a network of dairy cooperatives — was led by Verghese Kurien (often called the 'Father of the White Revolution', and famous for the Amul cooperative in Gujarat). (By contrast, the Green Revolution — in food grains — is associated with M.S. Swaminathan, the 'Father of the Green Revolution' in India.) The White Revolution transformed dairy farming and rural incomes. Understanding that Verghese Kurien led the White Revolution is a prelims point. The 'White Revolution' (Operation Flood), boosting milk production, was led by Verghese Kurien.

stem: The scientist regarded as the 'Father of the Green Revolution in India' is:
solution: M.S. Swaminathan is regarded as the 'Father of the Green Revolution in India'. An eminent agricultural scientist, he played a leading role in developing and introducing the high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds and the modern agricultural technology and practices that brought about the Green Revolution in India, making the country self-sufficient in food grains. (Verghese Kurien, by contrast, led the White Revolution in milk.) Understanding that M.S. Swaminathan is the father of India's Green Revolution is a prelims point. M.S. Swaminathan is regarded as the 'Father of the Green Revolution in India'.

stem: The land-reform movement in which Vinoba Bhave appealed to landowners to voluntarily donate part of their land to the landless was the __________ movement.
solution: The Bhoodan (meaning 'land-gift') movement — and its related Gramdan ('village-gift') movement — was the voluntary land-reform movement started by Vinoba Bhave (a follower of Mahatma Gandhi) in the 1950s. Bhave travelled across the country appealing to the big landowners to voluntarily donate a part of their land, out of goodwill, to be redistributed to the landless poor. It was a non-violent, moral appeal for land redistribution (rather than a government-enforced reform). Though it collected some land, its overall impact on land redistribution was limited. Understanding the Bhoodan movement (Vinoba Bhave's voluntary land-gift movement) is a prelims-relevant point. The Bhoodan (land-gift) movement, led by Vinoba Bhave, appealed to landowners to voluntarily donate land to the landless.

stem: The reform of tenancy laws (giving tenants security of tenure and regulating rents) was aimed at:
options: protecting the tenant cultivators from exploitation (by landlords) and giving them security and fair rents
solution: The reform of tenancy laws was aimed at protecting the tenant cultivators (those who farmed land rented from landlords) from exploitation, by: giving them security of tenure (protection from arbitrary eviction by the landlord, so they could not be thrown off the land at will); regulating and lowering the rents they had to pay (fixing fair rents); and, in some cases, giving them the right to eventually own the land they tilled. The aim was to improve the position of the tenant cultivators (who had been exploited under the old system) and to give them the security and incentive to invest in and improve the land. (Like other land reforms, tenancy reform had mixed success across states.) Understanding tenancy reforms (security of tenure, fair rents for tenants) is a prelims point. Tenancy reforms aimed to protect tenant cultivators by giving them security of tenure and fair, regulated rents.

stem: During the mid-1960s, India had a 'plan holiday' (a break in the Five Year Plans, replaced by three Annual Plans) mainly because of:
options: wars, droughts/famines, and a shortage of resources (economic crisis)
the end of all economic problems
a decision to stop planning permanently
solution: During the mid-1960s (1966–1969), India had a 'plan holiday' — a break in the sequence of Five Year Plans, during which three Annual Plans (one-year plans) were adopted instead. This was necessitated by a serious economic crisis and disruptions: the wars (with China in 1962 and Pakistan in 1965), which strained resources; severe droughts and food shortages/near-famine (mid-1960s); a shortage of financial resources and a foreign-exchange crisis (and the devaluation of the rupee in 1966); and general economic difficulties. These crises made it impractical to launch the Fourth Five Year Plan on schedule, so annual plans were used until the situation stabilised (the Fourth Plan then began in 1969). Understanding the 'plan holiday' of the mid-1960s (and its causes) is a prelims point. The mid-1960s 'plan holiday' (three Annual Plans) resulted from wars, droughts/famines, and a resource crisis.

stem: A justification for the government's (state's) large role and intervention in the economy during this period was that:
options: the private market alone would not undertake certain vital investments or ensure equity, so the state had to lead (correcting 'market failures' and promoting social goals)
solution: A justification for the government's large role and intervention in the economy (through planning, the public sector, and regulation) during 1950–1990 was that the private market, left to itself, would not achieve the country's development goals: the private sector was too weak and would not (or could not) undertake the large, risky, long-gestation investments needed in basic and heavy industries and infrastructure (so the state had to build these); and the free market would not ensure equity — it would tend to concentrate wealth and neglect the poor and backward regions/sectors (so the state had to intervene to promote social justice and balanced development). In economic terms, the state was to correct 'market failures' and to pursue social goals that the market would neglect. So state intervention was seen as necessary for both growth and equity in a poor, developing economy. Understanding the rationale for state intervention is a prelims point. The state's large role was justified as necessary because the private market alone would not make vital investments or ensure equity — the state had to lead and correct market failures.

stem: One achievement of the planning period was a significant rise in India's rate of __________ (which is needed to finance investment and growth).
solution: One important achievement of the planning period (1950–1990) was a significant rise in India's rate of savings and investment (as proportions of national income). At independence, savings and investment were very low; over the planning decades, they rose substantially (savings roughly tripled as a share of income). This was a real achievement, because a higher rate of saving and investment is essential to finance the capital accumulation needed for economic growth and development (as the Harrod-Domar model stressed). This rise in savings/investment helped build up the economy's capital base (industries, infrastructure). Understanding the rise in savings and investment as an achievement is a prelims point. A key achievement of the planning period was a significant rise in India's savings and investment rates.

stem: By the mid-1970s, India had achieved __________ in food grains (a major success of the planning/Green Revolution era).
options: self-sufficiency (no longer needing to import food grains)
solution: By the mid-1970s, India had achieved self-sufficiency in food grains — meaning it was producing enough food grains to meet its own needs and no longer had to depend on imports of food (or on food aid from abroad, like the earlier reliance on American PL-480 wheat). This was a major success of the planning era and, above all, of the Green Revolution (with its HYV seeds, fertilisers, and irrigation), together with the supporting policies (MSP, buffer stocks). Ending the chronic food shortages and import-dependence was a landmark achievement for the country's food security and self-reliance. Understanding that India achieved food-grain self-sufficiency by the mid-1970s is a prelims point. By the mid-1970s, India achieved self-sufficiency in food grains, a major success of the Green Revolution/planning era.

stem: Over the planning period, the structure of the economy changed as the share of the __________ sector in national income declined, while that of industry and services rose.
solution: Over the planning period (1950–1990), the structure of the economy changed: the share of the agricultural sector in national income (GDP) declined (from a little over half to a smaller proportion), while the shares of the industrial and services sectors rose. This structural shift — away from agriculture toward industry and services — is a normal feature of economic development (as an economy develops, agriculture's share falls and industry/services grow). However, in India, this shift in the share of national income was NOT matched by a corresponding shift in employment (agriculture continued to employ the bulk of the workforce), reflecting the limited job creation in industry. Understanding this structural change (falling share of agriculture in GDP) is a prelims point. Over the planning period, agriculture's share in national income declined, while industry's and services' shares rose.

stem: The type of farming in which farmers pool their land and resources to farm together (encouraged as part of agrarian reform) is called __________ farming.
solution: Cooperative farming is a system in which farmers voluntarily pool together (combine) their land, resources, and labour to farm collectively/jointly (as a cooperative), sharing the work and the produce. It was encouraged as part of the agrarian reforms, with the aim of overcoming the disadvantages of small, fragmented landholdings — by farming larger combined areas, farmers could use machinery and modern methods more efficiently, obtain inputs and credit more easily, and achieve economies of scale — while the farmers retained their ownership. (In practice, cooperative farming in India had only limited success, but cooperatives were very successful in areas like dairy — the White Revolution.) Understanding cooperative farming is a prelims point. Cooperative farming is where farmers pool their land and resources to farm together, encouraged to overcome the problems of small holdings.

stem: The industrial licensing system required an entrepreneur to obtain a government __________ before starting or expanding an industry.
solution: Under the industrial licensing system (a key feature of the regulated economy), an entrepreneur was required to obtain a government licence (permit) before starting a new industry, or before expanding, diversifying, or even changing the location of an existing industry. The government used this licensing power to control and direct industrial development — deciding who could produce what, how much, and where — in line with the plans (and to prevent the concentration of economic power, promote backward regions, etc.). But the system led to red tape, delays, favouritism, and corruption, and it stifled entrepreneurship and competition — which is why it was heavily criticised (the 'License Raj') and largely dismantled in the 1991 reforms. Understanding the industrial licensing requirement is a prelims point. The industrial licensing system required entrepreneurs to obtain a government licence to start or expand an industry.

stem: Small-scale industries were defined and given protection on the basis of a maximum limit on their __________.
solution: Small-scale industries (SSIs) were defined on the basis of a maximum limit on their investment (in plant and machinery) — a unit was classified as 'small-scale' if its investment in plant and machinery was below a specified ceiling (which was revised upward over time). Units within this investment limit qualified as small-scale and were given various forms of protection and support — such as the reservation of certain products for exclusive production by small-scale units, and concessions in taxes and credit — because small-scale industries are labour-intensive (generate a lot of employment) and help spread industry more widely (promoting equity). Understanding that SSIs were defined by an investment ceiling is a prelims point. Small-scale industries were defined by a maximum limit on their investment in plant and machinery.

stem: The subsidies given to farmers (on inputs like fertilisers, water, and electricity) are debated: supporters say they help farmers (especially the poor), while critics argue that subsidies:
options: are a huge burden on the government's finances, and often benefit the better-off farmers and encourage wasteful/harmful overuse of inputs
solution: The subsidies given to farmers (on inputs such as fertilisers, irrigation water, electricity, and credit) are a subject of debate. Supporters argue that subsidies are necessary to help farmers (especially small and poor farmers) by lowering their costs, encouraging them to adopt the new (Green Revolution) technology, and providing income support. Critics, however, argue that subsidies: place a huge burden on the government's finances (a large drain on the budget); often benefit the better-off, larger farmers (and prosperous regions) more than the poor; and encourage the wasteful and environmentally harmful overuse of inputs (e.g., excessive use of fertilisers and water, degrading the soil and depleting groundwater). So there are strong arguments on both sides of the farm-subsidy debate. Understanding the debate over farm subsidies is a prelims-relevant point. Critics argue farm subsidies burden government finances, mainly benefit better-off farmers, and encourage the wasteful overuse of inputs.

stem: A criticism of the planning strategy was 'export pessimism' — the belief that India could not increase its exports much, which led to a policy of:
solution: 'Export pessimism' was the belief (held by India's planners) that India could not significantly increase its exports (because, they thought, there was limited demand abroad for India's goods, and it could not compete). This pessimistic view led India to adopt an inward-looking strategy of import substitution — focusing on producing goods at home to replace imports, behind high protective barriers — rather than an outward-looking strategy of promoting exports. This neglect of exports (and of becoming internationally competitive) is now seen as a weakness of the strategy: it kept Indian industry inefficient and uncompetitive and led to chronic foreign-exchange shortages. (The contrasting, export-led strategy followed by the East Asian economies proved far more successful.) Understanding 'export pessimism' and its consequence (import substitution, neglect of exports) is a prelims point. 'Export pessimism' — the belief that India couldn't boost exports — led to an inward-looking import-substitution policy that neglected exports.

stem: The permit/licensing system and heavy controls are often blamed for encouraging __________ rather than genuine productive efficiency among businesses.
options: 'rent-seeking' — spending effort on obtaining licences/permits and favours (and corruption) rather than on improving production
solution: The permit/licensing system and the heavy government controls (the License Raj) are often blamed for encouraging 'rent-seeking' behaviour among businesses rather than genuine productive efficiency. 'Rent-seeking' means that, in such a controlled system, businesses found it more profitable to spend their effort, time, and money on obtaining the necessary licences, permits, quotas, and government favours (through lobbying, influence, and bribery/corruption) — since these permits (in a protected, restricted market) were the key to profits — rather than on actually improving their productivity, cutting costs, or innovating. This diverted energy into unproductive manipulation of the system (and bred corruption), instead of into productive, competitive enterprise. Understanding rent-seeking (a criticism of the License Raj) is a prelims-relevant point. The License Raj encouraged 'rent-seeking' — chasing licences, permits, and favours (and corruption) — rather than genuine productive efficiency.

stem: Despite the achievements of the planning era, a persistent problem that remained largely unsolved was:
options: widespread poverty and unemployment (a large section of the population remained poor)
solution: Despite the achievements of the planning era (food self-sufficiency, an industrial base, higher savings, etc.), a persistent problem that remained largely unsolved was widespread poverty and unemployment — a large section of the population (a huge number of people) remained poor and lacked adequate employment. The slow overall growth ('Hindu rate of growth'), the failure of the land reforms to redistribute land, the limited job creation in industry, and the rising population all meant that the benefits of development did not reach large sections of the people, and mass poverty and unemployment continued. Reducing poverty thus remained a central, unfulfilled challenge. Understanding that poverty/unemployment persisted is a prelims point. Despite the planning era's achievements, widespread poverty and unemployment persisted as a largely unsolved problem.

stem: The developmental strategy of 1950–1990 is credited with laying the foundation for later growth by building up India's:
options: basic and heavy industries, infrastructure, and a skilled/technical manpower and institutional base
solution: The developmental strategy of 1950–1990, whatever its shortcomings, is credited with laying an important foundation for India's later growth by building up: a base of basic and heavy industries (steel, machinery, chemicals, power, etc. — the industries needed to support further industrialisation); infrastructure (dams, power, transport, irrigation); a range of scientific, technical, and higher-educational institutions (like the IITs) that developed skilled and technical manpower; and various financial and institutional structures. This foundation of industry, infrastructure, and human capital, built during the planning era, provided the base on which the faster growth of the later (post-1991) period could be built. So the planning era's achievements had lasting value, even as its weaknesses had to be corrected. Understanding this 'foundation-building' contribution is a prelims-relevant point. The 1950–1990 strategy laid the foundation for later growth by building up basic and heavy industries, infrastructure, and skilled/technical manpower.

stem: Which pair is correctly matched (revolution and its field)?
solution: The correctly matched pair is: White Revolution — milk (dairy). The White Revolution (Operation Flood, led by Verghese Kurien) hugely increased India's milk production (dairy). Checking the others: the Green Revolution was in food grains (wheat and rice), NOT milk or fish. (For reference: Green Revolution → food grains; White Revolution → milk/dairy; Blue Revolution → fish/fisheries; Yellow Revolution → oilseeds.) Understanding the correct matching of these 'revolutions' with their fields is a prelims point. The White Revolution correctly refers to the growth of milk (dairy) production.

stem: The reason agriculture continued to employ the bulk of the workforce (even as its share in national income fell) was that:
options: the industrial and services sectors did not grow fast enough to absorb the workers, so surplus labour remained stuck in agriculture
there were no other jobs anywhere
solution: Even as agriculture's share in national income (GDP) fell over the planning period, agriculture continued to employ the bulk of the workforce because the industrial and services sectors did not grow fast enough (and were not labour-absorbing enough) to create sufficient jobs for the growing labour force — so the surplus labour remained stuck in (crowded onto) agriculture. In other words, the structural shift in output (away from agriculture) was NOT matched by a corresponding shift in employment. This meant a large workforce remained dependent on a low-productivity agriculture (with disguised unemployment), reflecting the failure to generate enough non-farm employment — a key weakness of the development strategy. Understanding this mismatch (falling GDP share but not employment share of agriculture) is a prelims point. Agriculture kept employing most workers because industry and services didn't grow fast enough to absorb them, leaving surplus labour in agriculture.

stem: Assertion (A): India adopted a mixed economy rather than a fully capitalist or fully socialist one. Reason (R): India wanted to combine the benefits of the market/private enterprise with a leading role for the state to ensure growth with equity, within a democracy. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India adopted a mixed economy — a middle path — rather than a fully capitalist (pure free-market) or a fully socialist (fully state-controlled/command) economy. And the reason is (R) that India wanted to combine the advantages of both systems: it wanted to keep the benefits of the market and private enterprise (efficiency, incentive, individual freedom), while also giving a leading, guiding role to the state (public sector, planning) so as to ensure rapid growth AND social equity (justice) and to protect the interests of the poor — all within a democratic framework (unlike the authoritarian command economies). So the desire to blend market and state to achieve growth with equity in a democracy is exactly why India chose a mixed economy — R correctly explains A. Understanding why India chose a mixed economy is a prelims point. India chose a mixed economy to combine the benefits of the market with a leading state role, achieving growth with equity within a democracy.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Indian Economy 1950–1990' is that:
options: In the decades after independence, India followed a path of planned development (Five Year Plans) with a mixed economy, aiming at growth with self-reliance and equity — achieving important successes (like the Green Revolution's food self-sufficiency, an industrial base, and abolition of intermediaries) but also suffering from serious weaknesses (an inefficient public sector, excessive controls/License Raj, and slow growth) that set the stage for the 1991 reforms
solution: The chapter conveys that, in the decades after independence (1950–1990), India pursued a path of planned economic development, through a series of Five Year Plans (formulated by the Planning Commission, set up in 1950), within the framework of a mixed economy (public and private sectors coexisting), guided by the goals of growth, modernisation, self-reliance, and equity. The strategy emphasised the leading role of the state and the public sector (especially in heavy/basic industries, following the Mahalanobis model of the Second Plan), self-reliance through import substitution (protecting domestic industry behind high tariffs and industrial licensing), the promotion of small-scale industries, and reforms in agriculture (land reforms — notably the abolition of intermediaries — and the Green Revolution). This approach achieved important successes: the Green Revolution made India self-sufficient in food grains; a diversified industrial base and infrastructure were built up; the intermediaries (zamindars) were abolished; and there was a shift toward more balanced development. But it also suffered from serious weaknesses: an over-regulated economy (the 'License-Permit-Quota Raj'), which bred inefficiency, red tape, and corruption; an inefficient and loss-making public sector; industries that were often inefficient and uncompetitive (due to excessive protection); the neglect of exports; and overall slow growth (the so-called 'Hindu rate of growth') and persistent poverty and unemployment. These weaknesses eventually led to the economic crisis and the major economic reforms of 1991 (liberalisation). Understanding the strategy, achievements, and shortcomings of India's planned development from 1950 to 1990 is the central concern of this chapter. From 1950 to 1990, India pursued planned, mixed-economy development aiming at growth with self-reliance and equity — with real successes (food self-sufficiency, an industrial base) but also serious weaknesses (an inefficient public sector, over-regulation, slow growth) that led to the 1991 reforms.
